rankedConcepts.objective: Escalate renal fluid removal when progressive major hypoxemia persists despite actual diuretic treatment.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Editorial prediction of a consequential general-surgery ICU decision. No exam percentage or observed difficulty is asserted.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Major hypoxemia worsens despite escalated IV loop treatment with negligible urine response.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Another pharmacologic trial can delay effective removal during respiratory deterioration.

rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Repeat potassium remains controlled after treatment, pH improved, and current respiratory and fluid needs are stable.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unnecessary replacement exposes the patient to treatment-related hemodynamic and access burdens.

rankedConcepts.objective: Adjust net removal separately from needed solute support when current circulation indicates intolerance of ultrafiltration.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Editorial prediction of a consequential general-surgery ICU decision. No exam percentage or observed difficulty is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Stop net removal while retaining currently needed solute support.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: MAP improves after net removal pauses and potassium control remains dependent on solute treatment.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Stopping all support loses needed clearance. Pressor-driven removal can worsen perfusion intolerance.

rankedConcepts.objective: Validate compromised pressure acquisition before choosing abdominal decompressive escalation.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Editorial prediction of a consequential general-surgery ICU decision. No exam percentage or observed difficulty is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Prioritize a repeat transvesical measurement using a specified physiological acquisition over a different diagnostic pathway.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: The only pressure was acquired during coughing, head elevation and excessive bladder filling.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Treating an unreliable value as established can drive incorrect invasive escalation.

rankedConcepts.objective: Use fluid anatomy to select an initial decompressive route after valid pressure-associated organ deterioration.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Editorial prediction of a consequential general-surgery ICU decision. No exam percentage or observed difficulty is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Use the accessible fluid anatomy to choose the initial decompressive route.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Large accessible free fluid remains, with no separate current surgical source-control indication.
rankedConcepts.consequence: An immediate open-abdomen intervention may be avoidable if targeted fluid drainage relieves the pressure component.

rankedConcepts.objective: Choose a circuit anticoagulation strategy when repeated clotting and recent hemorrhage compete.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Editorial prediction of a consequential general-surgery ICU decision. No exam percentage or observed difficulty is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Choose regional circuit anticoagulation with metabolic monitoring.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Repeated early clotting persists despite checked access and the current course supplies no demonstrated citrate intolerance.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Repeated circuit loss can compromise delivery, while systemic anticoagulation can aggravate bleeding risk.

rankedConcepts.objective: Choose a monitored interruption when actual off-treatment control and spontaneous urine support recovery despite residual creatinine elevation.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Editorial prediction of a consequential general-surgery ICU decision. No exam percentage or observed difficulty is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Choose continued monitored trial off support over automatic restart or modality conversion.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Actual off-treatment potassium, pH, fluid balance and support remain controlled as spontaneous urine rises.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Automatic restart may prolong support, while an unmonitored stop can miss recurrent needs.

rankedConcepts.objective: Select a current volume-response assessment when recurrent postoperative oliguria follows measured losses while pulmonary fluid findings persist.

proposedNodes.task: Which treatment should Nadia Ellis receive now for her low urine output?

choices.label: Give intravenous furosemide
choices.rationale: Accumulated fluid, lung findings and challenge nonresponse favor a monitored diuretic attempt.
choices.temptation: Treat the current congestion while assessing diuretic response.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Accumulated fluid, lung findings and challenge nonresponse favor a monitored diuretic attempt.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: New external losses with improved lung findings and a response to volume would favor replacement.

choices.label: Give an isotonic crystalloid bolus
choices.rationale: The observed volume challenge supplied no circulatory or urine benefit while fluid and lung findings accumulated.
choices.temptation: Equate oliguria with intravascular depletion.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: The observed volume challenge supplied no circulatory or urine benefit while fluid and lung findings accumulated.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: A perfusion deficit after external losses with a response to volume would favor a bolus.

choices.label: Begin continuous venovenous hemodialysis
choices.rationale: A diuretic attempt remains reasonable at this respiratory and metabolic stage before extracorporeal removal.
choices.temptation: Escalate automatically because creatinine doubled.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: A diuretic attempt remains reasonable at this respiratory and metabolic stage before extracorporeal removal.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Major hypoxemia persisting after adequate diuretic treatment would favor replacement.

proposedNodes.explanation: The record favors fluid accumulation without benefit from further expansion. An IV loop-diuretic trial addresses the volume problem, with reassessment of urine output and breathing. Its purpose here is decongestion.

twoConsequentialSteps.interpret: Integrate weight gain, lung observations and actual fluid-challenge nonresponse.
twoConsequentialSteps.apply: Choose a monitored diuretic attempt before extracorporeal removal.

proposedNodes.objective: Select a current volume-response assessment when recurrent postoperative oliguria follows measured losses while pulmonary fluid findings persist.

items.label: Interval output and intake
items.value: During the last eight hours after furosemide, urine output was 1.0 L, nasogastric output was 1.4 L and IV intake was 1.0 L. Urine output has now fallen again.

items.label: Current examination
items.value: Weight remains above the preoperative value. Leg edema and bilateral lung B-lines persist. Oxygen remains at 2 L/min, while MAP has fallen from 76 to 66 mmHg.

items.label: Kidney observations
items.value: Creatinine is 2.0 mg/dL and potassium is 4.5 mmol/L. The urinary catheter remains patent.

proposedNodes.task: Which assessment should guide Nadia Ellis’s next volume-management decision for recurrent oliguria?

choices.label: Measure stroke-volume response during passive leg raising
choices.rationale: Recent external losses and persistent pulmonary fluid findings leave the current response to additional volume unresolved. A reversible preload assessment measures the information needed for the next volume decision.
choices.temptation: Determine current volume responsiveness while avoiding another irreversible fluid challenge.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Recent external losses and persistent pulmonary fluid findings leave the current response to additional volume unresolved. A reversible preload assessment measures the information needed for the next volume decision.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: With stable volume balance and new urine blood/protein suggesting a renal parenchymal mechanism, fresh sediment assessment would take priority.

choices.label: Examine fresh urine sediment by manual microscopy
choices.rationale: Sediment can inform an intrinsic renal differential, but it does not establish the immediate circulatory response to volume under the competing current loss and lung findings.
choices.temptation: Attribute worsening creatinine and oliguria to a new intrinsic lesion before resolving the present volume decision.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Sediment can inform an intrinsic renal differential, but it does not establish the immediate circulatory response to volume under the competing current loss and lung findings.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Matched intake/output, stable circulation and new urine blood/protein would favor sediment assessment.

choices.label: Measure paired urine and serum urea for FEUrea
choices.rationale: A fractional-excretion result has limited ability to establish the current treatment response and does not directly measure the output response to preload.
choices.temptation: Use a urinary index as a substitute for functional circulatory assessment after a diuretic.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: A fractional-excretion result has limited ability to establish the current treatment response and does not directly measure the output response to preload.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: A broader renal-etiology evaluation after the immediate perfusion question is resolved may include urinary chemistry interpreted with the clinical course.

proposedNodes.explanation: The measured outputs exceed intake, yet lung fluid findings persist. These observations leave a consequential current volume question. Passive leg raising with direct stroke-volume or cardiac-output assessment can test preload responsiveness reversibly. Interpret its result with perfusion need and pulmonary risk before choosing treatment.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Removed the authored replacement-deficit conclusion and the already successful fluid challenge. All three labels are specific assessments with comparable length. The task names the real volume-management decision, and every choice could contribute to an AKI evaluation. No treatment response or volume-status interpretation is supplied.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStage: All choices are assessments before the next volume-management treatment. Urinary indices and sediment compete as etiologic approaches, while the key measures the current physiological response.

twoConsequentialSteps.interpret: Combine measured net losses, persistent lung fluid and changing MAP to recognize that neither the prior congestion state nor a urinary index settles present volume responsiveness.
twoConsequentialSteps.apply: Select a reversible direct output-response assessment before committing to further volume or removal.

manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted fair moderate. The nearest error is pursuing an intrinsic-renal workup or urinary index while the unresolved immediate decision concerns a potentially fluid-responsive component and pulmonary risk. No hard rating is claimed.

oneBestAnswer.decidingObservation: Substantial measured external loss coexists with continuing pulmonary fluid findings and a falling MAP, with no current challenge response supplied.
oneBestAnswer.errorConsequence: An etiologic test can leave the immediate volume decision unresolved. An empiric fluid or diuretic choice can worsen one side of the competing physiology.
oneBestAnswer.withoutDecider: Removing the simultaneous loss and pulmonary-risk observations removes the reason to prioritize this functional assessment. The originally included FENa was deleted because it did not change the prior treatment key.
oneBestAnswer.counterfactual: Replace this interval with matched intake/output, stable circulation and clear lungs, together with newly positive urine blood and protein. Fresh urine-sediment microscopy becomes the relevant next assessment among the offered choices.

manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Actual intake and both output streams permit the learner to establish net loss. Persistent weight, edema and B-lines preserve the competing lung-risk boundary. MAP supplies a current perfusion change. Creatinine, potassium and catheter patency establish the renal course and immediate context. FENa and an already successful fluid challenge were removed.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceCueAttack: The preceding PASS item and its feedback stay exact. They establish the earlier congestion state, but the new measured output/intake and current examination require reassessment. This follow-up assesses a different information need.
manualAuthorGate.repairsAndRecheck: Replaced the easy repeated-treatment item with an assessment decision. This materially changes the scored objective, so the new concept points to the previous concept without transferring history. Checked all assessments against the present stage and solved the stated alternative-course counterfactual.
manualAuthorGate.remainingRisk: The revised assessment ranking requires independent review. One directly retrieved expert commentary supports the precise passive-leg-raise technique. The source provides no universal treatment rule from a positive response.

proposedNodes.task: Which plan should guide Evan Brooks’s kidney-replacement decision at this assessment?

choices.label: Repeat chemistry and fluid-balance assessment
choices.rationale: Serial assessment can detect recurrence while cause-directed care continues after the observed response.
choices.temptation: Distinguish injury severity from current support need.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Serial assessment can detect recurrence while cause-directed care continues after the observed response.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: A recurrent treatment-resistant complication would favor starting replacement.

choices.temptation: Start replacement automatically for marked creatinine elevation.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: The current response and organ course do not establish an immediate need despite the severe creatinine rise.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Persistent dangerous hyperkalemia or major refractory pulmonary fluid accumulation would favor replacement.

choices.label: Perform a furosemide stress test
choices.rationale: Prognostic response testing does not replace assessment of current complications and their response.
choices.temptation: Use a prognostic maneuver as a dialysis-initiation test.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Prognostic response testing does not replace assessment of current complications and their response.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: A selected patient whose clinical question concerns progression risk may undergo prognostic assessment.

proposedNodes.explanation: Potassium and pH have improved and remain controlled at this assessment. Repeat chemistry and balance assessment addresses recurrence risk while cause-directed kidney care continues. The creatinine rise describes injury severity but does not independently establish an immediate extracorporeal support need.

choices.label: Set net removal to zero and continue clearance
choices.rationale: The circulation improves when removal pauses, while solute control still depends on treatment.

choices.lessAppropriateHere: The circulation improves when removal pauses, while solute control still depends on treatment.

choices.lessAppropriateHere: The actual response supports intolerance of current removal despite residual total-body fluid burden.

proposedNodes.objective: Choose a circuit anticoagulation strategy when repeated clotting and recent hemorrhage compete.

items.label: Bleeding course
items.value: Reoperation controlled a postoperative bleed. Drain output remains blood-stained and red-cell support was needed recently.

items.label: Circuit course
items.value: Two anticoagulant-free circuits clotted early and interrupted treatment. Access flow and catheter position have been checked.

items.label: Current metabolism
items.value: He is off vasopressors. Lactate is 1.3 mmol/L, bilirubin is 0.8 mg/dL and systemic ionized calcium is within the local reference range.

proposedNodes.task: Which CRRT anticoagulation strategy should Owen Carter receive now?

choices.label: Use regional citrate anticoagulation
choices.rationale: The repeated circuit loss makes an unanticoagulated strategy problematic, while the bleeding course makes systemic heparin less attractive.
choices.temptation: Preserve circuit patency while limiting systemic anticoagulant exposure.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: The repeated circuit loss makes an unanticoagulated strategy problematic, while the bleeding course makes systemic heparin less attractive.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Documented metabolic intolerance to citrate could favor an unanticoagulated or other specialist-directed strategy.

choices.label: Use systemic unfractionated heparin
choices.rationale: Systemic heparin adds systemic anticoagulation during the current bleeding-risk course.
choices.temptation: Prioritize filter life without adequately weighting recent hemorrhage.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Systemic heparin adds systemic anticoagulation during the current bleeding-risk course.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: A separate systemic anticoagulation indication with acceptable bleeding risk can favor heparin.

choices.label: Continue anticoagulant-free CRRT
choices.rationale: This avoids anticoagulant exposure but has repeatedly lost circuits despite checked access.
choices.temptation: Treat bleeding risk as a reason to accept any interruption burden.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: This avoids anticoagulant exposure but has repeatedly lost circuits despite checked access.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: High citrate-intolerance risk with adequate unanticoagulated circuit survival could favor this strategy.

proposedNodes.explanation: Regional citrate can preserve circuit patency while limiting systemic anticoagulant exposure in this bleeding-risk course. Metabolic monitoring is required. The current choice depends on both hemorrhage risk and the observed failure of anticoagulant-free circuits.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three standard strategies have parallel short labels. No availability sentence or pre-answer safety conclusion selects citrate. Actual metabolic observations establish the relevant boundary.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStage: One current circuit-anticoagulation choice. The key has no uniquely complete monitoring bundle.

twoConsequentialSteps.interpret: Weigh recent hemorrhage against actual repeated circuit failure after access assessment.
twoConsequentialSteps.apply: Choose regional circuit anticoagulation with metabolic monitoring.

manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate. The closest error is treating recent bleeding as an absolute reason to tolerate repeated unanticoagulated failures.

oneBestAnswer.decidingObservation: Repeated early clotting persists despite checked access and the current course supplies no demonstrated citrate intolerance.
oneBestAnswer.errorConsequence: Repeated circuit loss can compromise delivery, while systemic anticoagulation can aggravate bleeding risk.
oneBestAnswer.withoutDecider: Without actual circuit failure, continued unanticoagulated treatment becomes a stronger competitor.
oneBestAnswer.counterfactual: Supply prior documented citrate accumulation and adequate unanticoagulated circuit survival. Continue anticoagulant-free CRRT.

manualAuthorGate.repairsAndRecheck: Removed citrate-availability wording and moved monitoring rationale out of the key. Rechecked the competing risks.
manualAuthorGate.remainingRisk: Independent reviewer and Melissa must judge the clinical ranking and difficulty of this exact context.

choices.label: Continue the current trial off CRRT

choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: An observed recurrent metabolic or fluid-removal need favors restarting support.

choices.label: Restart the previous CRRT prescription

choices.lessAppropriateHere: The on-treatment creatinine included extracorporeal removal. The observed interruption does not establish a support need requiring automatic restart.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Recurrent dangerous hyperkalemia or pulmonary fluid accumulation during the interruption favors restarting support.

withheldTeachingPoints.boundary: Observational studies use different urine cutoffs, diuretic contexts and success durations. No universal threshold or guaranteed liberation interval is supported here.
withheldTeachingPoints.nextAction: Keep the response-based draft and obtain a specific adequate source before teaching a universal cutoff.

namedAlternatives: Use CRRT to delay required decompression
Proceed to decompression after failed less invasive measures
withheldTeachingPoints.boundary: Retrieved WSACS guidance does not establish renal replacement as a substitute for required abdominal decompression or establish a universal abdominal-perfusion pressure target.
withheldTeachingPoints.nextAction: Keep unsupported pressure targets and replacement-substitution claims out of scored teaching.

namedAlternatives: Percutaneous peritoneal catheter drainage
Decompressive laparotomy with temporary closure
Owner approvals needed.evidenceBoundary: Single-guideline GRADE 2D preference. The exact draft supplies accessible free fluid, new organ dysfunction and no separate re-exploration indication.
Owner approvals needed.questionForMelissa: For this exact pressure, organ trajectory and fluid anatomy, is catheter drainage a defensible first key, or should immediate decompressive laparotomy be keyed?

namedAlternatives: Zero net removal with continuing clearance
Interrupt the entire extracorporeal treatment
Owner approvals needed.evidenceBoundary: Current panel opinion supports stopping UF with hypovolemia findings. The draft supplies response to pausing removal and loss of potassium control with clearance interruption.
Owner approvals needed.questionForMelissa: Are these exact responses sufficient to key zero net removal with continued clearance, or should the stated instability require interruption of all treatment?

namedAlternatives: Reduce citrate load during shared corrective care
Immediately stop citrate and change strategy
Owner approvals needed.evidenceBoundary: The 2023 consensus supports reduction first and a strategy change if ineffective. The current 2025 guideline corroborates risk and monitoring without directly ranking this exact first adjustment.
Owner approvals needed.questionForMelissa: Does this exact calcium/perfusion pattern support the drafted initial reduction, or should immediate cessation be required?

namedAlternatives: Approve the exact reviewed clinical version
Request changes or retain a held key
Owner approvals needed.evidenceBoundary: All case headers, profiles, concepts, claims, keys and explanations are AI-assisted drafts. Author checks and structural validation retain separate roles.
Owner approvals needed.questionForMelissa: Which exact versions have defensible keys, realistic close alternatives and intended resident difficulty?

namedAlternatives: Continuous kidney replacement with gradual clearance
Adapted low-clearance intermittent or sustained low-efficiency treatment
Owner approvals needed.evidenceBoundary: Current guidance supports low-clearance therapy but does not universally rank all adapted intermittent or hybrid regimens below CRRT. The former qualifier-based set was withdrawn.
Owner approvals needed.questionForMelissa: Which patient-specific renal prescription comparison should distinguish continuous support from adapted low-clearance intermittent or hybrid therapy while preserving one defensible key?

namedAlternatives: Additional catheter drainage of the remaining accessible fluid
Decompressive laparotomy with temporary closure
Owner approvals needed.evidenceBoundary: A genuine residual target removes the easy foil, but the retrieved guidelines do not resolve the exact repeat-drainage versus operation ranking during this deteriorating course.
Owner approvals needed.questionForMelissa: For this exact partial-drainage anatomy and organ trajectory, should another targeted catheter or operative decompression be the immediate key, and what supported discriminator resolves that comparison?

Assess current need for replacement using actual treatment response despite a severe creatinine rise.
Escalate renal fluid removal when progressive major hypoxemia persists despite actual diuretic treatment.

Validate compromised pressure acquisition before choosing abdominal decompressive escalation.
Use fluid anatomy to select an initial decompressive route after valid pressure-associated organ deterioration.
Escalate to operative decompression after actual failure of less invasive measures and loss of the drainable fluid target.
Choose a circuit anticoagulation strategy when repeated clotting and recent hemorrhage compete.
Reduce citrate exposure after a calcium and perfusion trajectory supports accumulation.
Choose a monitored interruption when actual off-treatment control and spontaneous urine support recovery despite residual creatinine elevation.

sourceReview.title: Oliguria with postoperative fluid accumulation
fairness: IV furosemide is the best offered treatment for the accumulated fluid and new oxygen requirement after a nonresponsive fluid challenge. The stable circulation, potassium and pH make immediate kidney replacement less compelling. This does not imply that diuretics reverse the kidney injury.

Two consequential steps remain: integrate weight, lung findings and measured challenge response to identify the current fluid problem, then choose a diuretic trial rather than more expansion or immediate extracorporeal support. Fluid responsiveness and immediate replacement need are distinct judgments.

The negative challenge is legitimate observed response, not a wording-only cue. The three short treatment options have comparable specificity; no unique overlap, absolute, convergence or diagnosis-label shortcut was found.
This first node is self-contained with its named age/sex presentation and exhibit. Its explanation does not disclose the later FENa interpretation.

Review scope for all entries: offline editorial assessment of candidate Presentation, Current update, Exhibit, Task, Options and Explanation, including preceding visible nodes; author self-assessments and review-only key position were not evidence of quality. High-yield and difficulty labels are qualitative judgments, not verified examination-frequency or performance claims. PASS is not clinical approval or source verification; every draft still needs Melissa Rowland's exact clinical review. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in this node.
suggestions: Optional wording refinement: ask which fluid-management treatment she should receive, so the task does not imply that increasing urine output itself is the therapeutic goal. Preserve the explanation's explicit decongestion distinction.

The report covers all 11 new executable nodes; there are no rewritten or kept executable items in this packet. The withdrawn intracranial-modality candidate, its held unkeyed slot and three withheld teaching points are noted but receive no executable-node verdict.

cues.why: This authored conclusion directly selects 'Replace losses with isotonic crystalloid'; recognizing the word relationship requires no interpretation of FENa.

cues.why: This is legitimate clinical evidence, but combined with resolved oxygen need, near-baseline weight and explicitly under-replaced losses it makes repeating the successful action nearly automatic. Deleting the entire FENa result leaves the same obvious answer.

fairness: Controlled crystalloid replacement is the best offered answer. FENa obtained after furosemide cannot independently establish the cause of AKI; a high value does not negate the observed fluid-responsive course. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The serial case coherently reverses the earlier fluid state, and the current exhibit contains enough of the preceding treatment and response to stand on its own with the header. Prior feedback does not directly teach the FENa answer.

Both the renewed furosemide and immediate CRRT options are weak after the explicit replacement deficit and successful fluid challenge. The item tests a useful reassessment principle, but not two substantial resident-level steps.

Rebuild the closest competing plan so interpretation of the diuretic-exposed urine result actually changes the decision, rather than adding FENa to an already solved fluid-replacement vignette. Reapply the deletion test to that result.

sourceReview.title: Kidney-replacement need after medical treatment response
fairness: Repeat chemistry and fluid-balance assessment is the best offered immediate plan after current potassium and acid-base improvement, stable breathing and near-even balance. A marked creatinine rise establishes injury severity but is not by itself an immediate dialysis indication.

The two decisions are to distinguish the initial severe abnormalities from the present treatment response, then choose surveillance for recurrence rather than immediate replacement or a prognostic stress test. The furosemide stress test is a credible confusion between predicting progression and deciding current support need, although weaker than the dialysis alternative.

The options are concrete and similarly brief; the key is not uniquely qualified with an explanatory safety claim. Normal current findings are necessary to assess immediate indications rather than arbitrary negatives deleting unrelated diagnoses.

The first node stands alone. Its explanation gives a general decision principle but does not name the subsequent refractory-pulmonary-fluid answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. The unspecified interval after potassium treatment does not justify assuming durable recovery; the selected monitoring plan appropriately leaves recurrence open.
suggestions: Retain serial reassessment in the key and explanation; do not turn these constructed potassium or creatinine values into universal dialysis cutoffs.
Keep the distinction between prognostic testing and immediate support need explicit in post-answer feedback if feedback is expanded.

sourceReview.title: Escalation after failed diuresis and worsening hypoxemia
fairness: Urgent extracorporeal fluid removal is the best offered escalation given accumulating fluid, major hypoxemia, negligible urine response to escalated IV therapy and continuing respiratory deterioration. Adding a thiazide is a credible diuretic-resistance strategy, but pursuing another pharmacologic trial as the next definitive treatment risks delay in this course.

The learner must connect the fluid/respiratory trajectory to current support need and judge when the observed treatment failure outweighs another diuretic strategy. Distinct treatment classes are clinically necessary alternatives, not a lexical odd-one-out cue by themselves.

The item supports initiation of kidney replacement, not a universal preference for continuous venovenous hemodialysis over every intermittent or hybrid modality. The explanation appropriately limits the scored claim to escalation.

The second node follows the initially controlled course coherently and supplies enough current kidney, lung and treatment-response information to stand alone with the header. Earlier feedback does not give the exact answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

sourceReview.title: Separate net fluid removal from solute clearance
fairness: Setting net removal to zero while continuing clearance is the best offered prescription change: circulation improves when removal pauses, whereas potassium control still depends on clearance. Stopping all support and forcing continued removal with more pressor represent distinct, plausible errors.

The two consequential judgments are that current net removal is poorly tolerated despite the earlier pulmonary indication, and that this does not remove the separate need for solute treatment. The observed response supplies necessary evidence; it does not explicitly announce the combined prescription.

The choices have comparable length and specificity. The correct plan's two components do not uniquely arise from majority-component convergence: both continuing and stopping treatment components occur in the alternatives, and the physiology is still needed to choose the combination.

suggestions: Keep this as a reassessed prescription change rather than an absolute instruction that every hypotensive patient on CRRT must have zero net removal.

clarityIssues: 'Next renal-support decision' is less specific than the actual question: the immediate investigation of rising abdominal distension, oliguria and ventilator pressure. It can sound like a dialysis-prescription task.
'Standardized acquisition' names a quality goal rather than the concrete repeat-measurement procedure. The feedback identifies the faults but does not teach the correct acquisition method.

cues.phrase: Repeat transvesical pressure with standardized acquisition
cues.why: Only this option carries an explicit quality-assurance qualifier. A test-wise reader can select the standardized redo of the prominently described first measurement without knowing which acquisition features invalidate it.

fairness: Repeating the bladder measurement with proper technique is the best offered investigation in this currently blood-pressure-stable patient. Coughing, position and the large instilled volume compromise interpretation; CT or renal ultrasound does not validate the pressure measurement.

The intended two steps are real: recognize acquisition limitations, then prioritize validation over a different diagnostic pathway. The clinical concept is high yield, but the quality qualifier weakens the delivered discrimination.
This first node is self-contained. Its explanation correctly avoids announcing which intervention the later fluid-anatomy findings will select. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: Ask which investigation should be obtained next for the evolving abdominal and organ-function findings.

Replace 'with standardized acquisition' with concise concrete acquisition wording, keeping the other investigation labels comparably specific. Do not simply rename the key 'properly' or 'correctly' performed measurement.

Teach the supported acquisition method after the answer, including positioning, respiratory phase, bladder instillation and zero reference; verify any exact protocol values through the existing clinical-review process rather than inventing them.

dispositions.response: Aligned the task with the actual evolving findings, replaced the unique quality qualifier with a concrete procedure, and added the supported supine, relaxation, respiratory-phase, instillation-limit and zero-reference method in feedback. Re-solved CT in the counterfactual with already adequate pressure acquisition.
dispositions.openIssue: Moderate difficulty is retained after all identified clarity and qualifier issues were addressed. Manager must preserve the v1 context of the passed drainage item and keep this revised branch separate.

sourceReview.title: Initial drainage of an accessible abdominal fluid component
fairness: Catheter drainage is a defensible best initial option for the large accessible free-fluid component in the supplied sequence, which last describes stable blood pressure and improving postoperative bleeding/source-control observations. Laparotomy is a credible close alternative in pressure-associated organ dysfunction; it must remain available if drainage is inadequate or the clinical course demands urgent surgery.

The learner must interpret valid elevated pressure together with organ changes, then use the fluid anatomy and current surgical course to choose an initial decompressive route. The 'safe percutaneous window' is necessary access information distinguishing two real procedures, not gratuitous permission that should simply be deleted.

Current readings and observations make this node intelligible with its header. The prior node supplies the stable blood-pressure context and teaches measurement validity, not catheter drainage. If this node is delivered independently of that prior context, current hemodynamics should be repeated before asking for an invasive treatment ranking.

No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. Offline review does not establish a universal catheter-before-laparotomy rule or the certainty of that comparative recommendation. Exact clinical endorsement of the initial-drainage ranking remains with Melissa; unchanged hemoglobin, clear drains and falling lactate are reassuring observations, not proof that every surgical source-control concern is excluded.
suggestions: Preserve the complete prior course or explicitly include current circulatory stability in any standalone delivery.

Keep the feedback conditional on this accessible fluid component and reassessment; do not generalize it to all abdominal compartment presentations or imply that drainage may delay necessary operative decompression.

sourceReview.title: Persistent pressure-associated organ failure after drainage

cues.phrase: Repeat ultrasound now shows little free peritoneal fluid
cues.why: Against 'Place another percutaneous peritoneal drainage catheter', this is an explicit absence of the proposed target. It is clinically necessary evidence, but makes that alternative a conspicuously defeated repeat rather than a close next decision.

cues.phrase: Perform decompressive laparotomy with temporary closure
cues.why: This is the only newly escalated direct intervention after the preceding node already offered the same three strategies, selected drainage and explained the pressure-related organ problem. The sequence plus elimination of further drainage makes the key apparent before substantial new reasoning.

fairness: Urgent decompressive laparotomy is the best offered answer for persistent high pressure with anuria, worsening ventilation and increasing pressor need after the stated measures. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The escalation is coherent and the current exhibit supplies the previous drainage result, unsuccessful measures and current deterioration, so it stands alone with the header. In sequence, however, the earlier explanation has already supplied the pressure-related diagnosis and the need to reassess drainage.

The raw safety findings must stay. The weakness is difficulty: further drainage lacks a target and CRRT is an indirect response to an immediately worsening abdominal constraint. This is a valuable emergency-recognition decision, but the delivered alternatives do not require two consequential independent steps.
suggestions: Seek explicit acceptance as an easy safety/escalation node if this exact emergency-recognition purpose is desired.

If moderate/hard resident reasoning remains required, rebuild the decision around a real remaining clinical competitor whose eligibility is resolved by the current observations. Do not manufacture uncertainty by hiding the organ deterioration or failed measures.
Re-review the whole three-node sequence after revision; changing only this task wording will not undo the earlier diagnostic scaffold.

dispositions.response: One v2 attempt replaced the defeated catheter foil with an actual residual target. Re-solved all three plans. Two direct actions remained defensible under the low-certainty boundary, so the attempt was parked with an empty key.
dispositions.openIssue: Melissa must select the clinically supported repeat-catheter versus operative strategy or a different supported discriminator. The parked draft supplies no scored key.

sourceReview.title: Circuit anticoagulation after hemorrhage and repeated clotting
fairness: Regional citrate is the best offered strategy when recent bleeding makes systemic heparin undesirable and repeated anticoagulant-free circuit loss compromises treatment. The current perfusion and metabolic observations do not describe a clear citrate-intolerance state.

The resident must weigh ongoing bleeding risk against the actual failure of avoiding anticoagulation, then select a regional strategy using the current metabolic context. The choice is common practical ICU knowledge; it is moderate rather than hard for a resident familiar with CRRT.

The three labels are parallel and similarly brief. 'Two anticoagulant-free circuits clotted early' legitimately challenges continuing the same strategy; the observation does not identify citrate without knowledge of the systemic-versus-regional tradeoff.

The first node is self-contained. Its explanation calls for metabolic monitoring without disclosing the specific later calcium pattern or treatment change. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. Normal lactate and bilirubin must not be taught as a guarantee of citrate safety; the explanation appropriately retains monitoring.
suggestions: Keep the actual bleeding and circuit-loss history, and preserve metabolic monitoring in feedback.
Do not replace the raw metabolic observations with an authored declaration that the patient is 'eligible for citrate'; that would supply a consequential inference.

sourceReview.title: Calcium divergence and deterioration during citrate CRRT
clarityIssues: 'Arterial pH falls' and 'increasing vasopressor requirements and lactate' establish direction but not the severity or pace of the new deterioration. That matters if the intended distinction is reducing citrate versus stopping its exposure.
The task confines the answer to changing 'citrate infusion' and offers only three directions, so it does not test a complete response to the potentially serious complication.

cues.phrase: Which change should be made to Owen Carter’s citrate infusion now?
cues.why: After an adverse metabolic course, the task names the suspected treatment lever. With only 'Reduce', 'Increase' and 'Maintain' that infusion, a reader can favor reducing the implicated treatment without working through the calcium relationship.

cues.phrase: Reduce the citrate infusion rate / Increase the citrate infusion rate / Maintain the citrate infusion rate
cues.why: This directional option set supplies no strong competing mechanism or management strategy. Recognizing an adverse effect and reducing its named exposure is a recall chain, not two consequential clinical decisions.

fairness: The total-to-ionized calcium ratio rises from 2.0 to 3.5, with falling ionized calcium despite escalating replacement and worsening perfusion/acidemia. This supports citrate accumulation rather than merely an isolated calcium replacement deficit.

Reducing citrate exposure is directionally defensible, and no confident clinical falsehood is asserted here. However, the severe supplied calcium abnormality and worsening course make cessation a clinically important alternative that is not offered. Offline review cannot establish whether a reduction-only infusion plan is sufficient for this exact trajectory; that boundary requires clinical review rather than an invented cutoff.

The second node follows the earlier citrate choice coherently and restates treatment, new infection and the relevant laboratory course. It stands alone with the header; prior feedback mentions monitoring but does not reveal accumulation or the specific response. The shared continuation of calcium/perfusion treatment is useful and avoids a uniquely comprehensive key.
suggestions: Ask for a concrete next CRRT/anticoagulation strategy, with parallel competing plans representing accumulation, inadequate calcium replacement or another genuinely plausible interpretation; keep shared supportive care in the stem.

Have Melissa resolve whether reducing or stopping citrate is the best action for the exact supported severity and trajectory. Supply the decision-critical clinical information and avoid implying that merely reducing the rate is always sufficient.

Make interpretation of the total-versus-ionized calcium relationship necessary to distinguish the competing plans, and explain that relationship after the answer without inventing a universal treatment threshold.

dispositions.response: One v2 attempt added decision-critical pace, moved to complete competing circuit plans and retained common supportive care. The reduction-versus-cessation boundary remained unresolved, so all isCorrect fields and the key are empty and the item is parked.
dispositions.openIssue: Melissa must choose cessation versus reduced citrate for this exact supported trajectory before a keyed strategy version is authored.

sourceReview.title: Monitored liberation from CRRT despite creatinine rebound
clarityIssues: The task says 'now at the end of this CRRT circuit', but the exhibit says 'The circuit has been stopped for eight hours'. The decision is at reassessment during an interruption, not at circuit completion.

cues.phrase: Continue the interruption with chemistry and balance monitoring
cues.why: Only the key expressly includes surveillance and is appreciably more elaborated than either dialysis alternative. Its distinctive caution and the exhibit's 'Actual interruption' wording create an avoidable test-taking advantage, although physiology is still needed for a confident answer.

fairness: Continuing a monitored trial off treatment is the best offered plan given spontaneous urine, current off-treatment metabolic control, matched balance and stable support needs. The rise from an on-circuit creatinine value is not by itself proof that replacement must restart.

The two consequential steps are to interpret creatinine after extracorporeal clearance ends, then judge current endogenous control and choose a monitored trial rather than automatic resumption or modality substitution. This is high-yield practical renal-support reasoning.

The case stands alone and the clinical course is otherwise coherent. Neither eight hours off therapy nor the stated daily urine volume establishes a universal liberation threshold; the explanation appropriately rests on the combined current observations. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: Change the task to ask which kidney-support plan she should receive at this reassessment after CRRT interruption.

Put ongoing chemistry, fluid-balance and clinical monitoring in shared context, then compare similarly brief support plans. Preserve that stopping therapy is a monitored trial, not a declaration of completed recovery.
Keep both the on-circuit/off-circuit creatinine comparison and actual off-treatment observations; they supply the useful reasoning and should not be replaced by a 'kidneys have recovered' label.

dispositions.response: Repaired the timeline and the elaborated-key cue in one version. Re-solved the unchanged physiological key and the restart counterfactual after moving surveillance into shared care.
dispositions.openIssue: All identified clarity and surveillance-wording issues are addressed. Exact clinical review and independent re-review remain pending.

items.label: Clinical course
items.value: Abdominal distension, ventilator pressure requirements and creatinine have increased. Blood pressure remains stable.

items.label: First pressure record
items.value: A bladder pressure of 27 mmHg was recorded during coughing, with the head of bed elevated and 100 mL instilled into the bladder.

items.label: Urinary drainage
items.value: The catheter irrigates freely. The bladder is not distended on bedside assessment.

choices.label: Repeat transvesical pressure with standardized acquisition
choices.rationale: The displayed pressure needs technically reliable repetition using relaxed supine end-expiratory acquisition, correct zeroing and limited instillation.
choices.temptation: Validate decisive bedside data before escalating.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: The displayed pressure needs technically reliable repetition using relaxed supine end-expiratory acquisition, correct zeroing and limited instillation.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: An adequate pressure series with concern for an unresolved abdominal source could justify anatomical investigation.

choices.label: Obtain contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis
choices.rationale: CT may assess an abdominal source but does not resolve the flawed acquisition currently governing this pressure-related decision.
choices.temptation: Accept the displayed pressure and seek its anatomical cause first.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: CT may assess an abdominal source but does not resolve the flawed acquisition currently governing this pressure-related decision.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Reliable pressure data with concern for leak, hemorrhage or an unresolved lesion could favor CT.

choices.label: Obtain renal and urinary-tract ultrasonography
choices.rationale: Upper-tract imaging can address obstruction but leaves the present acquisition discrepancy unresolved.
choices.temptation: Anchor on a collecting-system cause of oliguria.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Upper-tract imaging can address obstruction but leaves the present acquisition discrepancy unresolved.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: An obstructive history without the current pressure-acquisition discrepancy could favor renal ultrasound.

priorNodes.explanation: The initial bladder reading needs technically standardized repetition. Coughing, position and excessive instillation compromise its interpretation. A valid series can then be related to the organ-function changes.

currentNode.task: Which decompressive intervention should Leah Morgan receive first at this assessment?

items.label: Repeat pressures
items.value: Two resting supine end-expiratory readings are 23 and 24 mmHg using 20 mL instillation and midaxillary zeroing.

items.label: Organ course
items.value: Urine output continues to fall and ventilator pressure requirements increase.

items.label: Abdominal assessment
items.value: Ultrasound shows a large free intraperitoneal fluid pocket with a safe percutaneous window and diffuse bowel-wall swelling.

items.label: Interval surgical course
items.value: Hemoglobin is unchanged without further transfusion. The drains return clear fluid and lactate has fallen after source control.

choices.label: Place a percutaneous peritoneal drainage catheter
choices.rationale: The large accessible fluid component offers a targeted initial decompressive route, followed by prompt reassessment.
choices.temptation: Use the current drainable anatomical component.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: The large accessible fluid component offers a targeted initial decompressive route, followed by prompt reassessment.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Little residual fluid with worsening organ dysfunction after drainage favors operative release.

choices.label: Perform decompressive laparotomy with temporary closure
choices.rationale: Operative release is important, but the current fluid anatomy permits a targeted initial drainage attempt under the society suggestion.
choices.temptation: Treat every overt pressure-related organ problem as requiring immediate open-abdomen management.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Operative release is important, but the current fluid anatomy permits a targeted initial drainage attempt under the society suggestion.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Persistent deterioration after less invasive treatment with little accessible fluid favors laparotomy.

choices.label: Begin CRRT with net fluid removal
choices.rationale: Renal support can address independent renal indications, but it does not directly drain the identified peritoneal component.
choices.temptation: Substitute systemic volume removal for a direct decompressive target.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Renal support can address independent renal indications, but it does not directly drain the identified peritoneal component.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: An urgent independent replacement indication can require renal support alongside abdominal care.

currentNode.explanation: Valid pressures and new renal and respiratory dysfunction establish a pressure-related organ problem. The large accessible peritoneal fluid component supports an initial catheter-drainage attempt. Pressure and organ responses require close reassessment.

reviewedItems.objective: Escalate to operative decompression after actual failure of less invasive measures and loss of the drainable fluid target.

items.label: Observed drainage
items.value: The catheter removed a large volume. Repeat ultrasound now shows little free peritoneal fluid and diffuse bowel-wall edema.

items.label: Current measures
items.value: Gastric decompression functions. Adequate analgesia and a brief neuromuscular-blockade trial have not lowered the pressure.

items.label: Current course
items.value: Resting bladder pressure remains 28 mmHg. Anuria, worsening ventilation and an increasing norepinephrine requirement develop.

reviewedItems.task: Which decompressive intervention should Leah Morgan receive now after catheter drainage?

choices.label: Perform decompressive laparotomy with temporary closure
choices.rationale: Pressure-related organ failure persists after the recorded less invasive measures. Operative release addresses the remaining abdominal constraint.
choices.temptation: Escalate using actual treatment response and current anatomy.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Pressure-related organ failure persists after the recorded less invasive measures. Operative release addresses the remaining abdominal constraint.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: A sizeable residual accessible fluid pocket with stable physiology might favor another drainage procedure.

choices.label: Place another percutaneous peritoneal drainage catheter
choices.rationale: The new map provides little target while organ function deteriorates.
choices.temptation: Repeat the formerly reasonable action without reassessing its result.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: The new map provides little target while organ function deteriorates.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: A large residual accessible collection with a pressure contribution could favor another catheter.

choices.label: Begin CRRT with net fluid removal
choices.rationale: Indirect systemic removal cannot substitute for necessary urgent abdominal decompression in this persistent overt course.
choices.temptation: Treat the remaining pressure problem as a total-body volume prescription issue.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Indirect systemic removal cannot substitute for necessary urgent abdominal decompression in this persistent overt course.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Independent renal-support need with improving abdominal pressure can justify a systemic removal adjustment.

reviewedItems.explanation: The drainable fluid has largely been removed, yet pressure and organ failures worsen despite the recorded measures. Decompressive laparotomy addresses the persistent abdominal constraint. The previous intervention must be reassessed using its actual result.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All labels name plausible decompressive strategies. Repeating the prior key is deliberately tempting. No option announces its own inadequacy. The update supplies a changed fluid map and response.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStage: Each option concerns the current decompressive intervention after the actual drainage trial.

twoConsequentialSteps.interpret: Recognize persistent pressure-associated failure despite the available less invasive response and changed anatomy.
twoConsequentialSteps.apply: Escalate to operative release.

manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate to hard. The resident must abandon a formerly appropriate intervention after new evidence.

oneBestAnswer.decidingObservation: Little drainable fluid remains while valid pressure, anuria, ventilation and pressor needs worsen.
oneBestAnswer.errorConsequence: Repeating low-yield drainage or relying on indirect removal can delay needed decompression.
oneBestAnswer.withoutDecider: Without the repeat map and current organ trajectory, another catheter remains credible and prior feedback could supply the answer.
oneBestAnswer.counterfactual: Supply a large remaining accessible fluid pocket and stable organ course after incomplete drainage. Another targeted catheter becomes reasonable.

manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: The repeat map changes the target. Actual drainage and medical measures establish what has occurred. Pressure and organ trend establish urgency. No mandatory elapsed waiting time is inserted.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceCueAttack: Prior feedback supported initial drainage and reassessment. It did not rehearse laparotomy after a failed response. The new observations earn the later decision.
manualAuthorGate.repairsAndRecheck: Removed a diagnosis label and an observation-only foil. Added a plausible systemic-removal competitor and re-solved the remaining anatomical problem.
manualAuthorGate.remainingRisk: Independent reviewer and Melissa must judge the clinical ranking and difficulty of this exact context.

reviewedItems.objective: Choose a circuit anticoagulation strategy when repeated clotting and recent hemorrhage compete.

items.label: Bleeding course
items.value: Reoperation controlled a postoperative bleed. Drain output remains blood-stained and red-cell support was needed recently.

items.label: Circuit course
items.value: Two anticoagulant-free circuits clotted early and interrupted treatment. Access flow and catheter position have been checked.

items.label: Current metabolism
items.value: He is off vasopressors. Lactate is 1.3 mmol/L, bilirubin is 0.8 mg/dL and systemic ionized calcium is within the local reference range.

reviewedItems.task: Which CRRT anticoagulation strategy should Owen Carter receive now?

choices.label: Use regional citrate anticoagulation
choices.rationale: The repeated circuit loss makes an unanticoagulated strategy problematic, while the bleeding course makes systemic heparin less attractive.
choices.temptation: Preserve circuit patency while limiting systemic anticoagulant exposure.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: The repeated circuit loss makes an unanticoagulated strategy problematic, while the bleeding course makes systemic heparin less attractive.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Documented metabolic intolerance to citrate could favor an unanticoagulated or other specialist-directed strategy.

choices.label: Use systemic unfractionated heparin
choices.rationale: Systemic heparin adds systemic anticoagulation during the current bleeding-risk course.
choices.temptation: Prioritize filter life without adequately weighting recent hemorrhage.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Systemic heparin adds systemic anticoagulation during the current bleeding-risk course.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: A separate systemic anticoagulation indication with acceptable bleeding risk can favor heparin.

choices.label: Continue anticoagulant-free CRRT
choices.rationale: This avoids anticoagulant exposure but has repeatedly lost circuits despite checked access.
choices.temptation: Treat bleeding risk as a reason to accept any interruption burden.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: This avoids anticoagulant exposure but has repeatedly lost circuits despite checked access.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: High citrate-intolerance risk with adequate unanticoagulated circuit survival could favor this strategy.

reviewedItems.explanation: Regional citrate can preserve circuit patency while limiting systemic anticoagulant exposure in this bleeding-risk course. Metabolic monitoring is required. The current choice depends on both hemorrhage risk and the observed failure of anticoagulant-free circuits.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three standard strategies have parallel short labels. No availability sentence or pre-answer safety conclusion selects citrate. Actual metabolic observations establish the relevant boundary.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStage: One current circuit-anticoagulation choice. The key has no uniquely complete monitoring bundle.

twoConsequentialSteps.interpret: Weigh recent hemorrhage against actual repeated circuit failure after access assessment.
twoConsequentialSteps.apply: Choose regional circuit anticoagulation with metabolic monitoring.

manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate. The closest error is treating recent bleeding as an absolute reason to tolerate repeated unanticoagulated failures.

oneBestAnswer.decidingObservation: Repeated early clotting persists despite checked access and the current course supplies no demonstrated citrate intolerance.
oneBestAnswer.errorConsequence: Repeated circuit loss can compromise delivery, while systemic anticoagulation can aggravate bleeding risk.
oneBestAnswer.withoutDecider: Without actual circuit failure, continued unanticoagulated treatment becomes a stronger competitor.
oneBestAnswer.counterfactual: Supply prior documented citrate accumulation and adequate unanticoagulated circuit survival. Continue anticoagulant-free CRRT.

manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Bleeding establishes systemic risk. Clotting after access assessment establishes the remaining circuit problem. Metabolic observations contribute to citrate-tolerance assessment.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceCueAttack: The later calcium trajectory and perfusion impairment are absent. Current feedback states monitoring needs without explaining the next answer.
manualAuthorGate.repairsAndRecheck: Removed citrate-availability wording and moved monitoring rationale out of the key. Rechecked the competing risks.
manualAuthorGate.remainingRisk: Independent reviewer and Melissa must judge the clinical ranking and difficulty of this exact context.

reviewedItems.objective: Reduce citrate exposure after a calcium and perfusion trajectory supports accumulation.

items.label: Interval course
items.value: He has received regional citrate CRRT. A new infection is accompanied by increasing vasopressor requirements and lactate.

items.label: Calcium trend
items.value: Total calcium rises from 2.2 to 2.8 mmol/L as systemic ionized calcium falls from 1.10 to 0.80 mmol/L.

items.label: Current support
items.value: The calcium infusion has required repeated increases. Arterial pH falls. Calcium correction and treatment of impaired perfusion continue with every proposed infusion choice.

reviewedItems.task: Which change should be made to Owen Carter’s citrate infusion now?

choices.label: Reduce the citrate infusion rate
choices.rationale: The diverging calcium measurements and increasing replacement needs during impaired perfusion support accumulation. Reduce the citrate load while shared corrective care continues.
choices.temptation: Interpret the calcium relationship before changing the citrate input.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: The diverging calcium measurements and increasing replacement needs during impaired perfusion support accumulation. Reduce the citrate load while shared corrective care continues.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Intact metabolism with inadequate circuit anticoagulation may support increasing citrate within a protocol.

choices.label: Increase the citrate infusion rate
choices.rationale: A greater citrate load may worsen the inferred accumulation.
choices.temptation: Treat falling pH as insufficient citrate-derived base without interpreting the calcium trend.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: A greater citrate load may worsen the inferred accumulation.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: Acidosis from inadequate base delivery without evidence of accumulation may require another citrate/base strategy.

choices.label: Maintain the citrate infusion rate
choices.rationale: Replacing calcium leaves the accumulating citrate load unchanged in this observed course.
choices.temptation: Attribute the falling ionized calcium entirely to replacement deficit.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Replacing calcium leaves the accumulating citrate load unchanged in this observed course.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: A verified calcium-delivery problem with preserved perfusion and a stable total-to-ionized relationship may favor maintaining citrate.

reviewedItems.explanation: Total calcium rises as ionized calcium falls and replacement needs increase during new perfusion impairment. This pattern supports citrate accumulation. Reduce exposure while correcting calcium and circulation, then reassess the metabolic course.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Three comparable labels vary the same infusion. The task does not name accumulation. The ratio remains uncalculated and uninterpreted. Shared calcium and perfusion care avoids a compound key.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStage: One citrate-rate adjustment at the current treatment phase.

twoConsequentialSteps.interpret: Infer accumulation from diverging calcium and escalating replacement needs during impaired perfusion.
twoConsequentialSteps.apply: Reduce citrate load while shared corrective treatment continues.

manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted hard. The close errors confuse accumulation with inadequate calcium delivery or inadequate base delivery.

oneBestAnswer.decidingObservation: Total calcium rises as ionized calcium falls despite increasing calcium delivery.
oneBestAnswer.errorConsequence: Treating the change as a replacement deficit can leave an accumulating citrate load in place.
oneBestAnswer.withoutDecider: Without the total-calcium trend, simple calcium under-replacement remains credible and reducing citrate is not established.
oneBestAnswer.counterfactual: Replace the course with a verified stopped calcium pump, stable total-to-ionized relationship and preserved perfusion. Maintain citrate while restoring calcium delivery.

manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: New perfusion impairment supports metabolic context. Paired calcium and replacement needs separate the nearest error. Falling pH makes the base-delivery error credible. Shared care preserves safety.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceCueAttack: The prior question tested patency versus bleeding. Its feedback supplied no calcium pattern, ratio or rate-adjustment rule.
manualAuthorGate.repairsAndRecheck: Changed a diagnosis-label question into an input adjustment. Moved calcium and perfusion correction into shared care, then re-solved the counterfactual.
manualAuthorGate.remainingRisk: The exact choice of reduction versus immediate cessation needs Melissa’s clinical review. One retrieved specialist consensus directly ranks this first adjustment.

reviewedItems.objective: Choose a monitored interruption when actual off-treatment control and spontaneous urine support recovery despite residual creatinine elevation.

items.label: Urine course
items.value: Urine output rose spontaneously to 1.6 L during the past day without diuretics. Net machine fluid removal was zero during the last shift.

items.label: Actual interruption
items.value: The circuit has been stopped for eight hours. Potassium changed from 4.3 to 4.5 mmol/L and arterial pH from 7.39 to 7.37.

items.label: Current balance
items.value: Intake and urine losses remain close to matched. Breathing and blood pressure remain stable without new support.

items.label: Creatinine
items.value: Creatinine rose from 1.1 mg/dL during treatment to 2.0 mg/dL during the interruption. Her pre-illness value was 0.8 mg/dL.

reviewedItems.task: Which kidney-support plan should Maya Reed receive now at the end of this CRRT circuit?

choices.label: Continue the interruption with chemistry and balance monitoring
choices.rationale: Spontaneous urine and the actual metabolic and volume course support a monitored trial despite residual dysfunction.
choices.temptation: Judge recovery against current support needs.
choices.lessAppropriateHere: Spontaneous urine and the actual metabolic and volume course support a monitored trial despite residual dysfunction.
choices.reasonableUnderCounterfactual: An observed recurrent metabolic or fluid-removal need favors restarting support.

choices.label: Restart CRRT at the preceding prescription

oneBestAnswer.counterfactual: Replace the interruption course with rising potassium despite medical treatment and increasing pulmonary fluid burden. Restart CRRT.

items.label: Current treatment

items.label: New course

items.label: Observed responses

answerChoices.label: Set net removal to zero and continue clearance
answerChoices.rationale: The circulation improves when removal pauses, while solute control still depends on treatment.

answerChoices.label: Continue net removal and increase norepinephrine

answerChoices.label: Stop solute clearance and net fluid removal
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied responses show an avoidable removal component and a remaining need for clearance.

reviewedNodeDefinitions.explanation: Perfusion improves when net removal pauses, while the observed potassium course still requires solute support. Set net removal to zero while continuing clearance and reassessing circulation. Future removal targets depend on that reassessment.

reviewedNodeDefinitions.stem: Which CRRT anticoagulation strategy should Owen Carter receive now?

items.label: Bleeding course
items.value: Reoperation controlled a postoperative bleed. Drain output remains blood-stained and red-cell support was needed recently.

items.label: Circuit course
items.value: Two anticoagulant-free circuits clotted early and interrupted treatment. Access flow and catheter position have been checked.

items.label: Current metabolism
items.value: He is off vasopressors. Lactate is 1.3 mmol/L, bilirubin is 0.8 mg/dL and systemic ionized calcium is within the local reference range.

answerChoices.label: Use regional citrate anticoagulation
answerChoices.rationale: The repeated circuit loss makes an unanticoagulated strategy problematic, while the bleeding course makes systemic heparin less attractive.

answerChoices.label: Use systemic unfractionated heparin
answerChoices.rationale: Systemic heparin adds systemic anticoagulation during the current bleeding-risk course.

answerChoices.label: Continue anticoagulant-free CRRT
answerChoices.rationale: This avoids anticoagulant exposure but has repeatedly lost circuits despite checked access.

reviewedNodeDefinitions.explanation: Regional citrate can preserve circuit patency while limiting systemic anticoagulant exposure in this bleeding-risk course. Metabolic monitoring is required. The current choice depends on both hemorrhage risk and the observed failure of anticoagulant-free circuits.

items.label: Interval course
items.value: He has received regional citrate CRRT. A new infection is accompanied by increasing vasopressor requirements and lactate.

items.label: Calcium trend
items.value: Total calcium rises from 2.2 to 2.8 mmol/L as systemic ionized calcium falls from 1.10 to 0.80 mmol/L.

items.label: Current support
items.value: The calcium infusion has required repeated increases. Arterial pH falls. Calcium correction and treatment of impaired perfusion continue with every proposed infusion choice.

answerChoices.label: Reduce the citrate infusion rate
answerChoices.rationale: The diverging calcium measurements and increasing replacement needs during impaired perfusion support accumulation. Reduce the citrate load while shared corrective care continues.

answerChoices.label: Increase the citrate infusion rate
answerChoices.rationale: A greater citrate load may worsen the inferred accumulation.

answerChoices.label: Maintain the citrate infusion rate
answerChoices.rationale: Replacing calcium leaves the accumulating citrate load unchanged in this observed course.

reviewedNodeDefinitions.explanation: Total calcium rises as ionized calcium falls and replacement needs increase during new perfusion impairment. This pattern supports citrate accumulation. Reduce exposure while correcting calcium and circulation, then reassess the metabolic course.

reviewedNodeDefinitions.stem: Which kidney-support plan should Maya Reed receive now at the end of this CRRT circuit?

items.label: Urine course
items.value: Urine output rose spontaneously to 1.6 L during the past day without diuretics. Net machine fluid removal was zero during the last shift.

items.label: Actual interruption
items.value: The circuit has been stopped for eight hours. Potassium changed from 4.3 to 4.5 mmol/L and arterial pH from 7.39 to 7.37.

items.label: Current balance
items.value: Intake and urine losses remain close to matched. Breathing and blood pressure remain stable without new support.

items.label: Creatinine
items.value: Creatinine rose from 1.1 mg/dL during treatment to 2.0 mg/dL during the interruption. Her pre-illness value was 0.8 mg/dL.

answerChoices.label: Continue the interruption with chemistry and balance monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Spontaneous urine and the actual metabolic and volume course support a monitored trial despite residual dysfunction.

answerChoices.label: Restart CRRT at the preceding prescription
answerChoices.rationale: The on-treatment creatinine included extracorporeal removal. The observed interruption does not establish a support need requiring automatic restart.

answerChoices.label: Convert to scheduled intermittent hemodialysis
answerChoices.rationale: Conversion still provides replacement when the current observations support assessing whether replacement is needed.

reviewedNodeDefinitions.explanation: The actual interruption shows spontaneous urine production with current metabolic and volume control. Continue a monitored trial off treatment.
